At this point is only wild especulation, but I just read about the
thread of the new set, and the "teaser" page on the VTES site from WW.
However discussing yesterday with a friend about this new set and what
it means for the future of VTES we thought of a theory.
A lot of people (as usual with any new set) do not like what they are
reading, and think this will disrupt the current status quo of the
game. Others, (myself included) are excited by this new set. I can
safely say that the phrase in the teaser "hunter crypt cards" bring the
biggest change on the game since the introduction of Events,(ok we had
a reflex, but really we already had cards with the same effect).
The theory we were thinking was that this is a really small set,
however big enough to support hunters completely, and maybe self
supported. Self supported in the sense that you'll have everything you
need to play the hunters as a hunter only deck or support with
vampires.
Now, how to please both type of players? those who hate the idea and
those who love it?.
If you hate the idea, then you don't have to buy this small set, as
there will not be anything of use to you. No new master for your usual
decks, no new ally you'd love to have, no vampire to complete your
crypt, as this is a "hunter set". And you'll have your usual new set in
the promised 9 months after the last normal set (in this case Legacies
of Blood). And as this set could be self contained, you won't have to
worry that the rare slot in you booster in next expansions will have a
hunter card.
If you love the idea, then you can buy the set, it is small enough that
it don't hit your pocket as hard as if it was a 150 cards set. It is
between the scheduled big expansions, and it will contain everything
you'll need.
So the players or playgroups can ignore having hunters with vampires or
include, based on a playgroup by playgroup basis.
Of course if this works it opens a whole new universe in VTES, why only
hunters? maybe next we'll have a 60 cards self cotnained Mummy set, or
demon (how would I wet my pants having the Hasmed crypt card), and the
same, you like it, you buy the specific set, you don't you just ignore
it as if it never existed.
Of course all of this is just especulation, but I don't think it is a
bad idea. Any thoughts?

for a years-dead RPG (not that I'm asking for such an explanation, yet.
Anything formulated today would be similarly nonsensical, owing to a lack of

Influence is a mechanism for the acquisition of resources, with which to
win a game of VTES. In the past, the only game resources you could acquire
through influence were vampires, and pool (indirectly, through drawing off
an Arcane Library, or somesuch). Soon, we have a new resource type which we
can field using the influence mechanic. In so much as these new resources
add an interesting twist to the game's dynamic, and preserves game play
balance (easily done with proper playtesting, IMO) I'm in favor of it.

either. Yes, previously, you could only get allies from actions to get

discard action. Things change. As long as this expansion isn't breaking

Sure. But in terms of game mechannics, there is nothing actually
special about the influence phase as a way to purchase resources that
prevents it from being used to get things other than vampires--I
realize that the rule book says something about "bringing your vampiric
power to sway over younger minions" or whatever, but in terms of how

> simply making these new hunters as ally cards as has been done in the
> past?

'Cause having to bring them into play with actions that can be
blocked/cancelled leads to having a whole deck concept shut down from
the get go. With "hunters" (whatever they end up being--I have
absolutely no pre-knowledge of this expansion) as crypt cards, you can
build a "hunter" based deck and, at the very least, not have to worry
about not being able to get the necesary minions into play by virtue of
the recruit action being blocked.

> Why risk game balance and game flavour if those cards could be
> represented with an existing mechanic at all?

Why risk game balance and game flavor over any new mechanic?

> Novelty, most likely. Otherwise known as a 'selling point' when you
> are marketing a product.

Sure. That this expansion introduces a new mechanic to the game
certainly is a selling point. I (and I'm likely not alone) am certainly
intrigued by the use of crypt cards to bring out allies.

> So why do you play this game?

'Cause it is a fantastic game. I never have never played the RPG. I
only know about the backstory 'cause I have picked up a few of the old
rulebooks used and at auctions, just to get some backstory so the VTES
cards make more sense. Like, I find the window dressing appealing, as,
like, I like monsters and vampires and stuff, but if the game had been
a science fiction game with the exact same mechanics (just different
names for stuff), I likely would have been just as sold on it when I
started playing.

> Is it not about Vampires, elders and
> fledglings, and the vampiric jyhad? Or just plain, you know, vampires?

Yeah, it is. But the vampires sometimes fight hunters. And I suspect
that the designers wanted to try out a new mechanic with crypt based
mortals as it made them more accessible (you don't need to wait till
they are in your hand and then have to recruit them to get them in
play) and probably more capable in general (depending on how they make
them work), but likely less capable than vampires. Maybe it will work
great. Maybe not. Maybe it will be a failled plan, and the whole idea
will cease to be an issue. Maybe it'll work great, be interesting and
balanced, and make the game more interesting. We'll see.

> Not resources plural, resource singular. Younger vampires.

Not any more.

> An assumption, yes. I can already see alot of cardtext issues arising
> from this. How they are dealt with could prove interesting and
> awkward. Hard to speculate on such game balance issues until the
> mechanic is revealed.

True. I suspect that the mechanics involved will be fairly simple, as
it is a booster only set, so no rulebook reprints. Perhaps all
mechanics will be dealt with via card text.

> All of one card iirc.

Sure. This is all of 20 cards. What is the difference, really?

> There are tons of ally focused decks. But decks without vampires to
> put them in play? That I have yet to see. And for a reason.

They exist. Based on the ally that comes into play via the master phase
(i.e. without him being recruited the normal way). They aren't real
good, but the are viable.

> Events required some form of new mechanic, that card type never existed
> before.
> But allies already have applicable card mechanics, so why screw with an
> existing one which serves a different purpose?

'Cause it allows the hunters to be better than library based allies.
The designers apparently thought it would be interesting to be able to
build a deck around mortal hunters with no vampires at all (which
already exist, but are harder to pull off). By making them crypt cards,
you don't have to wait to draw them and you don't have to not get
blocked recruiting them. Making build the all mortal deck much more of
a viable concept. But not necessarily any more successful--if they are
still suceptible to all the steal ally effects, and get killed when
they run out of life, and don't have much life to begin with, they are
hardly going to eclipse vampires. It seems more likely that they'll get
shuffled into vampire crypts that they fit into as spice or added
ability and they will show up in all hunter decks that aren't that
good.

> "Powerful" or not, someone will build the all ally/hunter deck, and I'm
> sure some new hunter card will warrant it. I have no desire to see
> that in a game called *vampire*.

Sure. But you can already do that. You can make pure ally decks that
influence out no vampires at all with Jake Washington. You can make,
say, War Ghoul decks that influence out 1 weenie vampire the whole game
and just brings out War Ghouls that do everything else. I've made
plenty of decks where the vampires were little more than an
afterthought and the allies did everything (hordes and hordes of
computer hacking Arms Dealers with .38s). Not good decks to be sure.
But they worked.

Now, we will be taking an already existing concept (vampireless or ally
focused decks) and making it more viable by adjusting an existing
mechanic. It'll probably be not *that* effective, though, and the
hunters will probably hang out with vampires more often than not.

-Peter

(say, if VTES was instead a game about giant fighting robots, you could
use the exact same mechanic, call it the "build phase", and bring giant
fighting robot cards into play in the exact same way). In a backstory
sense, assuming the influence phase represents the player "methuselah"
using their powers to influence vampires to do their bidding, why
couldn't the player "methuselah" use their powers to influence mortals
to do the same thing? Why would an ancient and powerful being need to
use a middle man (i.e. get a weaker vampire to do the influencing for
them by recruiting the ally)?

> You're joking right?

Nope.

> Ally decks that (by the ally card mechanic)
> require actions to put them into play are all shut down from the start
> by the nature of that mechanic? C'mon Peter, you're going nowhere with
> that line of logic.

Getting blocked recruiting an ally is a sure way to get an ally deck
not to work. If you are designing an expansion that the whole focus of
which is using mortal allies, it would make sense to me to want to
ensure that the mortal allies had no problem getting into play.

Making the hunters into crypt cards does a couple things that seperates
them from ally library cards:

A) It makes them a certain resource, as opposed to a possible resource.
Ally library cards require you drawing them and getting them into play,
both of which make them a crap shoot to rely on. Making them crypt
cards means that you can always draw them and always get them in play.

B) It makes them likely more powerful than library based allies. Again,
I have no pre-knowledge of these hunter cards, but by making them crypt
cards, it opens up a new avenue for rules to make the hunters more
capable than library based allies.

Assuming that you, as a designer, want to make an expansion that
focuses on hunter mortal allies, and you want to make it work well,
making the hunters crypt cards seems like the most obvious way to do
that.

I mean, like, I can accept that someone might not like the very basis
of the idea (i.e. making mortal hunters as the basis of a deck and an
expansion), but I don't find it remotely problematic.

> Because this is such a hurdle why exactly?

It is a hurdle if you want to be able to play a mortal hunter based
deck--having to rely on drawing and recruiting ally cards from your
library makes the concept of a mortal hunter based deck a questionable
plan. The designers, apparently, wanted people to be able to do this.
This being the case, hunter crypt cards become obvious.

> Well if they can be represented with an existing mechanic, I have no
> idea Peter. Kind of my point.

But thay can't necessarily be represented in the same way--that they
are crypt cards, again, makes them into a different kind of resource
than when they are library cards. They are recources that you can
reasonably build a deck around, assuming that you *will* have access to
them and *will* be able to get into play. Allies in the library are
sketchy to rely on.

> See its that 'better' that I have a real issue with. It makes the all
> ally deck 'better' and thus more likely to see play. Something that
> goes against the very concept of the game not to mention the original
> design. Ergo, repugnant to me.

I have no problem with hunter crypt cards or all mortal based decks
from either a design or a conceptual level. If they lead to interesting
game play, I'm all for them. Again, I'm assuming that the hunter crypt
cards are going to be mostly like the Bloodlines vampires--best used as
a thrown in sideline to a crypt of mostly vampires, but possible to
make a whole deck out of, although likely of questionable utility.
Which works for me.

> Sure. They still involved vampires. And clan specefic ones at that,
> which opens you up to various clan and contesting mechanics as well.
> Not something to ignore really.

Sure. But on a conceptual level, I'm not so much seeing the difference
between:

A) A deck that brings out only Horatio and uses him to recruit 5 War

Ghouls that do everything else.

B) A deck that is all allies all the time, and doesn't even bring out
Horatio.

-Peter

Messages.Author: CthuluKitty
Messages.Body:
> Crypts are quite undeveloped as far as a resource system or
> mechanically manipulated concept is concerned. It needs further

> developement, and this is a start. (by putting non-vampire cards into
> crypts).

What are you talking about? There's an entire phase devoted to
managing your crypt resources, which is among the most fundamental
elements of what makes Jyhad different from other card games. In
addition to the influence phase, there are 4 vampires and 22 library
cards that interact directly with the crypt--not to mention the
uncontrolled region, which sort of an extension of it.

In terms of developing the crypt (whatever that means), how does adding
non-vampire cards to it accomplish that? Adding more vampires would
have done precisely the same thing.

And why does anything in the game "need" further development? The game
works quite well as far as I've noticed.

Messages.Author: Tom Duncan
Messages.Body:
talonz wrote:
> > > And they can't accomplish this with current or future ally cards
> > > why...?

I would guess that it has to do with the power curve. The Ally
template has it's own costing established, and if the new allies are
Imbued or whatever, it might make dropping them from your hand too
expensive. Rampant speculation, from a business sense it also seems
like the logical next step for expanding the game. There is finite
material from which to build new product.

We've been co-habitating the PoB long enough for me to pick up on your
purism a bit, and I respect that, but from a thematic view it (non-vamp
crypt cards) makes sense. If a methuselah can "influence" powerful
vampires, why not powerful mortals? The game allows for the vampires
you control to recruit allies, why couldn't a methuselah (presumably
more powerful than the vampires he/she controls) recruit allies
directly? I think Jake Washington sets a precedent for this - just
moving it to another phase.

> elements of what makes Jyhad different from other card games. In
> addition to the influence phase, there are 4 vampires and 22 library
> cards that interact directly with the crypt--not to mention the
> uncontrolled region, which sort of an extension of it.
>

You can do only three things in the influence phase; move counters on,
move counters off, add a vampire to your uncontrolled region. That
seems quiet undeveloped to me, contrast that with the minion phase.
Although the master phase only lets you play master cards or use a
master phase action for a card in play, what you can do with a master
phase action is quiet broad. After events were added as a new option to
the discard phase, did you not see that other phases could be further
developed?

> In terms of developing the crypt (whatever that means), how does adding
> non-vampire cards to it accomplish that? Adding more vampires would
> have done precisely the same thing.
>

No, it would have added more vampire variety, and only a small
percentage of new variety since there are already lots of vampires. Now
a completely different minion type can be brought into play during your
influence phase.

> And why does anything in the game "need" further development? The game
> works quite well as far as I've noticed.

Because a game that stays stagnant will probably die. Sure Vampire
lasted many years with no new expansions, but it also did not make any
money for the publisher at that time. If White Wolf puts out expansions
with no new mechanics, eventually they will put out expansions that
look like previous expansions and no one (or fewer players) will buy
them.

Speculating that they want to grow the game of Vampire into the World
of Darkness.
